extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political theory, history, and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for designing or evaluating republican constitutions to prevent or control factional violence and majority oppression; discusses causes of faction and institutional remedies (representation, extent, structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to break and control the violence of faction
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed Union's chief advantage is its tendency to break and control the violence of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison frames controlling faction as the principal desideratum for a constitution: factions produce instability, injustice, and confusion in public councils. A good government should provide a proper cure for faction without violating the principles of liberty. (Original phrasing: "Among the numerous advantages promised by a well-constructed Union, none deserves to be more accurately developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Two general methods for curing faction: remove causes or control effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing causes would require either destroying liberty or making all citizens have the same opinions/interests; both are impracticable or unwise. Therefore the practical rubric is to focus on institutional designs that control the effects of faction rather than attempting to eliminate diversity of opinion or liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve liberty while addressing faction
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is essential to political life and cannot be sacrificed to cure faction; liberty is 'to faction what air is to fire'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any constitutional remedy must not abolish the very liberty that makes political society possible. Remedies that suppress liberty are worse than the disease of faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent a majority of citizens sharing the same passion/interest, or render such a majority unable to concert and execute oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the existence of the same passion or interest in a majority must be prevented; or the majority, having such passion, must be rendered, by number and local situation, unable to concert and carry into effect schemes of oppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central institutional test: systems should (a) lower the probability that a single interest will dominate a majority across the polity or (b) structure representation, size, and extent so that even a majority with common interest cannot coordinate and impose oppression. Moral or religious motives are unreliable controls when impulse and opportunity coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republic (representation) preferable to pure democracy for controlling factions
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic, where the government is delegated to a small number of citizens elected by the rest, refines and enlarges public views and promises a cure for faction that a pure democracy cannot provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation filters and refines public opinion through chosen representatives whose greater wisdom and patriotism may better discern national interest. However, representatives can be corrupted or captured, so the design must also minimize such risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent and multiplicity of interests (large republic) reduce likelihood and coordination of dominant factions
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater number of citizens and greater sphere of country make factious combinations less to be dreaded because they increase variety of parties and interests and make concert and execution of oppressive schemes more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending the sphere (a large republic or union) increases the number and variety of competing interests, reducing the chance that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade rights; it also creates practical obstacles to coordination and secret collusion across wide territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate size and number of representatives to balance local knowledge and national perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives must be numerous enough to guard against the cabals of a few, yet limited enough to avoid the confusion of a multitude; there is a mean between extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too few representatives risk localism and attachment to narrow interests; too many dilute national perspective and cause confusion. The Constitution (per Madison) strikes a practical balance by assigning local matters to states and aggregate interests to the national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger electorates make it harder for unworthy candidates to succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: Because each representative in a large republic is chosen by a greater number of citizens, it is more difficult for unworthy candidates to practice the vicious arts by which elections are often carried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A larger pool of electors increases the likelihood that merit and established character will prevail in elections, reducing election fraud, intrigue, and local factional capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of judge and party; avoid letting parties be judges in their own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: No man is allowed to be a judge in his own cause because his interest would bias his judgment; by the same token, bodies that are both advocates (parties) and judges of legislative determinations are unfit to decide in impartial fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative acts often function as judicial determinations over classes of citizens; constitutional design should include mechanisms to prevent the dominant party from using legislative power to oppress minority rights (checks, representation, structural limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize distribution of property and economic interests as primary sources of faction to be managed
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common and durable source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property; different classes (landed, manufacturing, mercantile, moneyed, creditors vs debtors) have distinct interests that naturally divide society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation of these various and interfering interests is a principal task of modern legislation; good constitutional structure should reduce opportunities for particular economic interests to dominate legislation to the public's detriment (e.g., through representation, division of powers, and large republic effects).
